_about: Hand-edited layer joined onto the SAM wiki extract by scripts/build.py. 'plain' is HCF wording drafted by Claude on 2026-10-21 (unreviewed). 'glossary' maps to health-glossary sleep entries (relation: same | overlaps | narrower = the glossary entry is a specific version of this item | conflicts). 'disagreements' only records positions that a named source states; nothing here is new evidence. Items with 'from' = 'glossary' are glossary entries with no wiki item, given a proposed place in the wiki's categories.

audienceTags.all-ages-and-cultures: Default. Fits anyone unless another tag narrows it.
audienceTags.adults: Written for adults; not checked for children.
audienceTags.children-and-teens: Evidence or advice specific to under-18s.
audienceTags.parents-and-caregivers: Acted on by someone caring for another person.
audienceTags.shift-workers: People who work nights or rotating shifts.
audienceTags.people-with-insomnia: Ongoing trouble falling or staying asleep.
audienceTags.people-who-snore-or-may-have-sleep-apnea: Loud snoring, gasping, pauses in breathing.
audienceTags.people-with-a-late-body-clock: Delayed sleep-wake phase: fall asleep and wake much later than wanted.
audienceTags.talk-to-a-clinician: Involves a supplement, medicine, device or condition; suggest checking with a health professional.
audienceTags.needs-money-or-equipment: Costs money or needs something many people do not have.
audienceTags.region-or-culture-specific: Comes from, or fits, a particular place or culture (see audienceNote).
audienceTags.infants: Babies under 1 year (advice acted on by caregivers).

items.plain: Go to bed and get up at about the same times every day.

disagreements.about: Which matters more, a fixed bedtime or a fixed wake time

positions.says: Keep both bedtime and wake time the same every day, weekends included (p. 28).
A steady wake time matters more than a steady bedtime.

items.plain: If you need to move your sleep times, shift them a little each day instead of all at once.
items.notes: The wiki item title says 'avoid drastic changes'; its practical tip is about shifting 15-30 minutes per night, which is the actionable version used for the plain line.

items.plain: Most adults need 7 to 9 hours; notice how much you need to wake up rested.
items.audienceNote: The wiki taxonomy labels this '8-hour rule (recommended in Asia)'; the regional claim has no citation. Children and teens need more sleep than adults; that is not covered here.

positions.says: Its own write-up says 7-9 hours is the guideline and that a strict 8-hour rule is 'overly simplistic' (wiki ref 106, Harvard Health), yet the item is named 'Follow the 8-hour rule'.

items.notes: Item name and its own evidence disagree. Suggest renaming the item; the plain line follows the evidence, not the title.

items.plain: If you nap, keep it short and before mid-afternoon.
items.audienceNote: Napping norms differ by culture (siesta cultures, workplace naps). Shift workers may need longer naps; see adjust-to-night-shift-work.

positions.says: A short nap can make up for lost sleep; napping after 3 p.m. can make it harder to fall asleep (p. 29).
After a late night, take a short afternoon nap rather than sleeping in.
Item 3.2.1 states 'Naps harm nighttime sleep' as a general claim; its own tip is to keep naps under 30 minutes and before 3 PM.
No naps (recorded in health-glossary#17 from his videos; not a glossary entry).

items.notes: Duplicate of wiki 3.2.1 (see notes there).

items.plain: Get up at the same time every day, weekends too.
items.notes: Listed in the wiki taxonomy with no write-up.

items.plain: Keep weekend wake-up times close to weekday ones; if you're short on sleep, a little extra on weekends may help.

disagreements.about: How much weekend sleep-in is OK

positions.says: No more than about an hour later than usual.
Sleeping later on weekends won't make up for lost sleep (p. 28); gives no limit.
Keep bedtime and wake time within the same hour every day, even on weekends.

items.notes: The wiki item says 'limit social jet lag'. The one-hour figure in the plain line is Huberman's and is unverified; see also myth M2. Plain line corrected after the literature search: NSF 2023 says catch-up sleep 'may be beneficial' when weekday sleep is short; no source supports the one-hour rule.
items.plainBefore: On weekends, wake up within about an hour of your weekday time.

items.plain: Keep your bedroom cool and dark at night.
items.audienceNote: Cooling tips assume a fan or air conditioning; hot climates and shared rooms make this harder.

positions.says: Item tip: 60-67°F (15-19°C). The wiki's Tools tab: 18-20°C.
About 65 to 72°F (unverified in the glossary notes).
Keep the room 'on the cool side' (p. 29); no number.

items.plain: Block light from windows with heavy curtains or an eye mask.
items.notes: Write-up has no citations.

items.plain: Sleep on a mattress and pillow that feel comfortable to you.
items.notes: Wiki name 'Invest in...' assumes money; the tip offers a mattress topper as a cheaper option. Write-up has no citations.

items.plain: If noise wakes you, try a fan or white noise to cover it.
items.notes: Overlaps 1.2.5 and 1.4.2 (pink noise). Write-up has no citations.

items.plain: Make your bedroom as quiet as you can, or use earplugs.
items.notes: Wiki page is a blank template. Earplugs in the plain line are an editorial addition, not from a source.

items.plain: Charge your phone and other devices outside the bedroom.
items.notes: Listed with no write-up. Related to 1.3.1; the NSF 2024 consensus found screen use harms sleep in children and teens, not adults (see 1.3.1).

items.plain: Keep your bedroom tidy so it feels calm.
items.notes: Listed with no write-up or evidence.

items.plain: Try a calming scent such as lavender at bedtime.
items.notes: Listed with no write-up or evidence.

items.plain: In the hour before bed, choose calm screen use or none, and keep phones out of children's bedrooms.
items.audienceNote: The NSF 2024 consensus found harm in children and teens; it did not reach consensus for adults. Keep a separate adult wording until adult evidence is checked.

disagreements.about: How strong the evidence is, and for whom

positions.says: Scores this 'strongly supported' (1 on red flags; 5/5 support in both summary tables) for everyone, and explains it mainly by blue light suppressing melatonin.

Consensus that screen use in general, and the content of pre-bedtime use, impair sleep in children and adolescents. The abstract reports no consensus for adults, or that pre-bedtime light impairs sleep.
The link runs both ways: people who can't sleep may use screens to pass time or calm down. How much it matters depends on how much, for whom, and which mechanism.
Blue light suppresses melatonin (also the wiki's myth M4 on TV).
Consensus on content harming children's and teens' sleep; no consensus on light.
Blue light delays melatonin, and stimulation from scrolling, shows or games keeps the brain alert. Tech curfew at least one hour before bed.

items.notes: This is the worked example in the Open Health Communication Declaration (vivwebsolutions/hcf-guides#6). The plain line is a first try at the nuanced version and needs Kalman's review. Wiki tip: a 'screen curfew' 30-60 minutes before bed.

items.plain: Do the same calm things in the same order before bed, like reading or a warm shower.
items.notes: Write-up has no citations.

items.plain: Save exciting or stressful activities for earlier in the evening.
items.notes: Overlaps 1.3.7 and 2.3.4. Write-up has no citations.

items.plain: If you wake at night, don't look at the clock.
items.notes: NHLBI (p. 30) says to turn the clock face away. Write-up has no citations.

items.plain: Try a guided sleep meditation or a mindfulness recording at bedtime.
items.notes: Listed with no write-up. Overlaps 3.1.2.

items.plain: Some people find a weighted blanket calming at night.
items.audienceNote: Not checked for children; weighted blankets carry safety warnings for infants and young children (warning not sourced here; check before publishing).
items.notes: Listed with no write-up or evidence.

items.plain: Leave hard conversations for earlier in the day when you can.
items.notes: Listed with no write-up. Overlaps 1.3.3.

items.plain: Take a warm bath or shower an hour or two before bed.

positions.says: 60-90 minutes before bedtime.
Before bed; no timing (p. 29).
A warm shower in the second 20 minutes of a one-hour wind-down, so 20-40 minutes before bed.

items.notes: Wiki scores ease 3 on the item page but 5 in both summary tables. Write-up has no citations.

items.plain: Pink noise is popular, but the evidence is weak, and one trial found it reduced dream (REM) sleep.
items.notes: Wiki's own scores disagree sharply on evidence (item page: 'well supported'; classification table: 'weak evidence', impact 1). Write-up has no citations. Plain line corrected after the literature search: Basner 2026 RCT found all-night pink noise cut REM sleep; earplugs blocked traffic noise.
items.plainBefore: Some people sleep better with pink noise, like steady rain, than white noise.

items.plain: If your feet get cold, wear loose socks to bed.
items.notes: Pulls the opposite way from cooling tips (1.2.1, frozen water bottle); the wiki says warm feet help the body shed heat. Write-up has no citations.

items.plain: Get outside in daylight soon after you wake up.
items.audienceNote: Hard for people who wake before sunrise, in high-latitude winters, or who can't go outside.

positions.says: At least 30 minutes of daylight a day; an hour of morning sun if falling asleep is hard (p. 30).
15 minutes.
About 5 minutes on a clear day, 10 cloudy, 20-30 overcast, within 30-60 minutes of waking, not through a window.
10-30 minutes, within an hour of waking.
Within 30 minutes of waking; no duration given.

items.notes: Wiki scores reach 3 on the item page but 5 in the summary table, and novelty 4 vs 1.

items.plain: Use dimmer, warmer lights in the evening.
items.notes: Wiki item says 'reduce blue light'. The NSF 2024 consensus did not reach consensus that pre-bedtime screen light impairs sleep; the plain line is about room light overall, not screen filters. Write-up has no citations.

items.plain: If you need light at night, use a dim red or amber one.
items.notes: Wiki scores disagree on evidence (item page: well supported; classification table: limited). Huberman's reason (cortisol) is unverified. Write-up has no citations.

items.plain: Turn the lights down little by little as bedtime gets closer.
items.notes: Wiki item names 'smart lighting'; the plain line drops the product. Listed with no write-up.

items.plain: Some people wear blue-light-blocking glasses in the evening.
items.notes: Listed with no write-up or evidence. See 2.1.2 for why the light mechanism is disputed.

items.plain: Have your last caffeine by early afternoon and your last big meal a few hours before bed.

positions.says: At least 6 hours before bed.
Effects can last up to 8 hours (p. 28); no clock time.
2 p.m.; half-life 6-8 hours.
No more than about 100 mg after 4 p.m.
Coffee only before 2 p.m.; homepage: 'by early afternoon'; caffeine lasts 6–8 hours.
2-3 hours before bed.
Stop eating 2 hours before (3-2-1 rule).
Avoid large meals late at night; a light snack is fine (p. 29).
Finish dinner 2–3 hours before bed; lighter snacks if hungry.

items.notes: NHLBI pairs caffeine with nicotine; the wiki has no nicotine item. Wiki splits alcohol into 2.2.3.

items.plain: Drink most of your fluids earlier in the day so you don't wake up to use the bathroom.
items.audienceNote: Not for people who need fluids at night for medicine, diabetes or thirst (caution from the glossary's 3-2-1 entry).

positions.says: Stop fluids 1 hour before bed (3-2-1 rule).
Item 2.5.3 suggests chamomile tea 30-45 minutes before bed.
Taper fluids after 8 pm; a small calming drink before bed is fine.

items.plain: Don't use alcohol to help you sleep; stop drinking a few hours before bed.
items.notes: Listed with no write-up; myth M1 covers the same ground with citations. '3 hours' is from the 3-2-1 rule, not a trial.

items.plain: Eat foods with enough magnesium; ask before taking a supplement.
items.notes: Listed with no write-up or evidence. Supplement safety not checked.

items.plain: Be active most days; it helps you sleep better.
items.notes: NHLBI: at least 30 minutes most days (p. 28).

items.plain: Try a few minutes of gentle stretching or yoga before bed.
items.notes: Write-up has no citations.

items.plain: If you do strength training, try it in the afternoon or early evening.
items.notes: Wiki scores disagree (classification table: reach 1, novelty 5; item page: reach 2, novelty 4). Write-up has no citations.

items.plain: Finish hard workouts at least an hour before bed; evening exercise is otherwise fine.

positions.says: Item title: 2 hours. Myth M3: at least 3 hours (wiki refs 86, 87).
2 to 3 hours (p. 28).
About 4 hours before bed (recorded in health-glossary#17 from his videos; not a glossary entry).

items.plainBefore: Finish hard workouts at least a couple of hours before bed.
items.notes: Plain line corrected after the literature search: Stutz 2019 and Frimpong 2021 find evening exercise fine, except vigorous exercise ending within about 1 hour of bed. Experts in Robbins 2019 rated 'exercise within 4 hours disturbs sleep' a myth.

items.plain: To wind down, breathe in for 4, hold for 7, and breathe out for 8.
items.notes: Wiki item says it 'can slow heart rate'; the glossary flags Breus's heart-rate claim as unverified. Write-up has no citations.

items.plain: Mouth taping is popular, but the evidence is thin; check with a clinician first.
items.notes: Wiki rates evidence weak-to-limited and impact low in its classification tables, but well supported on the item page. Safety for people with blocked noses or possible sleep apnea not checked; the plain line is cautious on purpose. The wiki's novelty-vs-reach section calls mouth taping 'strong scientific support but low commonality', which contradicts its own scores.

items.plain: Try slow breathing through your nose before sleep.
items.notes: Listed with no write-up.

items.plain: Some small studies found kiwi or tart cherry before bed helped sleep.
items.notes: Plain line hedged because the wiki write-up cites no studies and its classification table rates evidence 'limited'. Availability and cost vary by region.

items.plain: If you're hungry at bedtime, a small snack is fine.

positions.says: A small carb-rich snack 30 minutes before bed.
Avoid large meals late; a light snack is fine (p. 29).
Stop eating 2 hours before bed (3-2-1 rule).

items.notes: Wiki's serotonin reasoning is uncited.

items.plain: A cup of chamomile tea can be part of a calm bedtime routine.
items.audienceNote: Herbal products can interact with medicines; passionflower especially (not sourced here; check).

positions.says: Tea 30-45 minutes before bed.
No fluids in the last hour (3-2-1 rule).

items.notes: Wiki summary table rates evidence 5/5; item page rates it 'well supported'; the write-up cites nothing.

items.plain: Do something that calms you before bed when you're stressed.
items.notes: Broad; 3.1.2-3.1.4 are the specific ways to do it.

items.plain: Try slow breathing or meditation to relax at bedtime.
items.notes: Write-up has no citations.

items.plain: Tense and then relax each muscle group, one at a time, from feet to head.

positions.says: Start at the feet, tense 5-10 seconds.
5-7 seconds; starts at the toes in one video and the head in another.

items.plain: Write down what's on your mind, and one next step, before bed.

positions.says: Before bed.
A few hours before bed, so you are not holding it in bed.

items.notes: In the wiki's 'New Sleep Advices' list (not yet placed). No write-up.

items.plain: Short naps are fine for most people; long or late naps can make night sleep harder.
items.notes: The wiki item is a claim ('Naps harm nighttime sleep'), not advice, and its own evidence says it depends. Recommend merging into 1.1.4 and moving the claim to the myths list.

items.plain: Use your bed only for sleep and sex.
items.notes: Part of stimulus control (NHLBI calls it reconditioning therapy). Wiki tip folds in 3.2.3.

items.plain: If you can't sleep after about 20 minutes, get up and do something calm until you feel sleepy.

disagreements.about: Get up or stay in bed

positions.says: Get out of bed after about 20 minutes awake and do something relaxing (pp. 30, 37).
Stay in bed with the lights off and breathe slowly instead of getting up.

items.notes: Direct conflict between sources; the declaration's 'where sources disagree' field exists for cases like this. In the wiki's 'New Sleep Advices' list. No write-up.

items.plain: If your mind races, picture a string of random, unconnected things.
items.notes: Kept on purpose as niche-but-maybe-valuable (Kalman's v1.2 feedback). Wiki scores clash: classification table rates evidence 1 (weakest), item page rates it well supported, and the scatterplot text promotes it as 'practical but lesser-known'. Write-up has no citations.

items.plain: Before bed, write down three things you're thankful for.
items.notes: Wiki item says 'instead of a to-do list', which conflicts with 3.1.4 (write down worries and next steps). Write-up has no citations.

items.plain: Some people relax with binaural beats; evidence for sleep is mixed.
items.notes: Needs headphones. Wiki rates it 3 on red flags (mixed) on the item page. Write-up has no citations.

items.plain: Try nature sounds or ASMR recordings to relax at bedtime.
items.notes: In the wiki's 'New Sleep Advices' list. No write-up.

items.plain: If you get heartburn at night, try sleeping on your left side.
items.notes: Wiki summary table rates evidence 5/5; write-up cites nothing. Pregnancy advice about left-side sleeping is a separate topic, not covered.

items.plain: Some people relax with gentle massage or acupressure before sleep.
items.audienceNote: Acupressure points (P6) come from traditional Chinese medicine.
items.notes: Write-up has no citations.

items.plain: If you have reflux or sleep apnea, raising your upper body may help; ask your clinician.
items.notes: Wiki classification tables rate it 1 on everything (hardest, weakest); the item page rates it well supported with strong impact. Biggest internal spread in the wiki.

items.plain: Some people find raising their legs a little helps them feel comfortable at night.
items.notes: In the wiki's 'New Sleep Advices' list. No write-up or evidence; the circulation claim in the wiki title is not repeated.

items.plain: Write down when you go to bed, wake up and how you slept for a week or two.
items.notes: A sleep diary is the starting point for sleep restriction therapy and CBT-I. Write-up has no citations.

items.plain: If you can't fall asleep until very late, ask a clinician about timed melatonin or morning light.
items.notes: Wiki tip names a 10,000-lux box. Write-up has no citations. Plain line corrected after the literature search: AASM 2015 makes no recommendation for light therapy alone in adults with delayed sleep-wake phase, but weakly recommends timed melatonin.
items.plainBefore: If you can't fall asleep until very late, ask a clinician about morning bright-light therapy.

items.plain: Melatonin may help with jet lag or shift work; ask a pharmacist or doctor first.

positions.says: Discusses melatonin for jet lag but says the evidence is mixed (pp. 10-12).

items.audienceNote: Melatonin is sold over the counter in some countries and by prescription in others.
items.notes: In the wiki's 'New Sleep Advices' list. No write-up.

items.plain: If you snore loudly or gasp in your sleep, ask a doctor about sleep apnea.
items.notes: In the wiki's 'New Sleep Advices' list. No write-up; myth M5 (snoring) covers it with citations. The glossary has 'Sleep Apnea, Central' but no obstructive sleep apnea term yet.

items.plain: Ask your pharmacist or doctor whether any of your medicines can affect sleep.
For long-lasting insomnia, ask about CBT-I, a structured talking and habits treatment.
items.notes: The wiki's discussion tab names CBT-I as the intervention linking categories 3 and 4, but it has no item.

items.plain: With a clinician's help, limit time in bed to the sleep you actually get, then add time back.
items.notes: NHLBI caution: avoid driving or machinery while sleep-deprived during this process.

items.plain: Before a long trip, shift your sleep times a little toward the new time zone.
On night shifts, use bright light at work and a dark, quiet room to sleep in.
Some advise getting outside in late-afternoon light too.
items.notes: Huberman only; low confidence in the glossary. His protective claim is unverified and left out.

items.plain: Your body is coldest a couple of hours before you usually wake.
items.notes: A concept used in jet-lag advice, not advice by itself. The 2-hour figure is Huberman's and unverified.

items.plain: Breathe in for 4, hold for 4, out for 4, hold for 4, and repeat.
Breathe in fully through your nose, then breathe out slowly and completely.
Breathe slowly so your belly, not your chest, rises and falls.
Breathe in through one nostril and out the other, switching sides.
Lying still with your eyes closed rests you a little, but it is not a substitute for sleep.
items.notes: Pulls against 3.2.3 (get up after 20 minutes). Plain line corrected 2026-10-21 after the literature search: sleep experts rate 'lying in bed with eyes closed is almost as good as sleeping' a myth (Robbins 2019), and no study shows quiet wakefulness is restorative.
items.plainBefore: If you can't sleep, lying still with your eyes closed still rests your body.

items.plain: Use the last hour before bed for chores, then washing up, then something calm.
Stop alcohol 3 hours, food 2 hours and drinks 1 hour before bed.
items.audienceNote: Skip the fluid step if you need fluids for medicine, diabetes or thirst.

items.plain: On hot nights, a frozen water bottle wrapped in a sock can cool you down in bed.
items.notes: A personal trick; no evidence cited.

items.plain: Some advise waiting 90 minutes or more after waking for your first coffee.

positions.says: About 90 minutes, because cortisol drops by then (unverified).
90-120 minutes, to spread energy and want less caffeine later.

items.notes: Popular claim; evidence not checked.

items.plain: Pick a time in the early afternoon after which you have no caffeine.
items.notes: Specific version of 2.2.1; see its caffeine disagreement.

items.plain: If you're naturally a night owl or early bird, set your bedtime with that in mind.
items.notes: Evidence for tailoring bedtime to chronotype not checked. Breus's branded animal labels left out.

items.plain: One expert says to stay in bed and breathe slowly when you wake at night.
items.notes: Conflicts with 3.2.3 and NHLBI; kept so the disagreement is visible.

items.plain: After dark, keep indoor lights low and screens dim.
items.notes: Overlaps 2.1.2 and 2.1.4. Huberman's 10 p.m.-4 a.m. window is his rule of thumb.

items.plain: Stop work or schoolwork at least an hour before bed.
items.paragraph: Deadlines push us to sacrifice rest, but the late-night work rarely pays off the next day. Finishing earlier allows the brain to settle and restores clarity for tomorrow.
items.notes: Not in the wiki or glossary. Do One Thing commitments give 9 pm and one hour as examples.

items.plain: Plan get-togethers earlier in the day so late nights are the exception.
items.paragraph: Connection is vital, but it doesn’t need to cost tomorrow’s energy. By shifting when and how we socialize, we keep both joy and rest intact.

items.sourceWording: I will stretch or move my body every morning to signal the day has begun.
items.plain: Stretch or move your body soon after you wake up.
items.notes: Body-clock reasoning ('signal the day has begun') is not cited.

items.sourceWording: I will use an alarm clock instead of relying on my phone.
items.plain: Use an alarm clock instead of your phone, so the phone can stay out of the bedroom.

items.sourceWording: If poor sleep persists for more than a few weeks, talk with a professional — you don’t have to navigate it alone.
items.plain: If poor sleep lasts more than a few weeks, talk with a health professional.
items.paragraph: Anxiety and depression can complicate sleep, but simple practices and self-compassion change the tone of nights.
items.notes: From the homepage quick tips and the Mental Health Conditions commitments.

positions.says: If poor sleep persists for more than a few weeks.
If changes to sleep habits have not helped and you've had trouble sleeping for months (per the guidelines search).

items.sourceWording: I will give myself grace on rough nights. / I will see poor sleep not as failure but as feedback.
items.plain: After a bad night, go easy on yourself; one rough night is feedback, not failure.
items.notes: A mindset item. Worry about sleep itself keeps people awake; that reasoning is not cited here.

items.plain: If you use cannabis, keep it away from bedtime and notice how it affects your sleep.
items.audienceNote: Legal status differs by country and state.
items.paragraph: Cannabis affects sleep differently for everyone, but heavy use often suppresses restorative REM cycles. Reflection and moderation bring clarity.
items.notes: The REM claim is Do One Thing's and is not cited. Not in the wiki or glossary.

items.plain: Get plenty of bright light during the day, and keep your nights dark.
Sleep tips alone rarely fix long-lasting insomnia; if poor sleep goes on for months, ask about CBT-I.
items.notes: Frames the whole dataset: most items here are sleep hygiene tips, which AASM 2021 advises against as the only treatment for chronic insomnia.

items.plain: Don't try to split your sleep into several short blocks a day to need less sleep.
items.literatureMatch: cut your sleep into several short blocks
items.notes: Polyphasic sleep (NSF 2021 consensus).

items.plain: Teens' body clocks run later; support later school start times instead of blaming teens for sleeping late.
items.notes: Policy-level advice.

items.plain: Put babies to sleep on their backs, on a firm flat surface, in your room but not in your bed.
items.literatureMatch: Put babies to sleep on their back

items.plain: If trying hard to fall asleep keeps you awake, stop trying and let sleep come on its own.
items.literatureMatch: If trying hard to fall asleep
items.notes: Paradoxical intention and acceptance-based approaches.

items.plain: Listening to calm music for 25 to 60 minutes at bedtime may help you sleep better.
items.notes: Better evidence (Cochrane 2022) than binaural beats, pink noise or ASMR.

items.plain: Falling asleep anywhere, any time is a sign you're short on sleep, not a sign of good sleep.
Hitting snooze for a short while is fine for most people.
items.notes: Evidence is mixed: experts in Robbins 2019 vs a 2024 RCT.

items.plain: Melatonin isn't automatically safe for children and teens just because it's natural; ask a clinician first.
From about 28 weeks of pregnancy, go to sleep on your side (left or right), not on your back.
items.notes: Evidence does not favor left over right; one cohort (Silver 2019) found no link.

items.plain: For older adults, sleeping pills usually help only a little and raise the risk of falls and confusion; try other approaches first.
Avoid smoking or vaping in the evening; if you quit, sleep may be rough for a few weeks before it improves.
items.notes: NHLBI pairs nicotine with caffeine (see caffeine-and-big-meals-early).

items.plain: A pet in the bedroom is usually fine; if it wakes you, keep it off the bed.
Sharing a bed is fine for most couples; if a partner's snoring wakes you, get the snoring checked or try separate beds.
items.literatureMatch: Sharing a bed with a partner

items.plain: Be wary of sleep advice from popular videos and influencers; check it against a health service or sleep society.
Use a sleep tracker lightly, if at all; it can't diagnose sleep problems, and if the numbers make you worry, stop.
If your snoring or apnea is worse on your back, sleeping on your side may help; ask your clinician.
items.literatureMatch: sleeping on your side may help

M1.plain: Alcohol may make you drowsy, but it makes sleep worse later in the night.

M2.plain: Sleeping in on weekends doesn't fully make up for short sleep during the week.

M3.plain: Regular exercise helps sleep, but hard workouts right before bed can keep you up.

M4.plain: Falling asleep to TV can make sleep lighter and more broken.
M4.notes: Wiki explains this with blue light; see 1.3.1 for why the light mechanism is disputed.

M5.plain: Loud, frequent snoring can be a sign of sleep apnea and is worth checking.
